hero.name: Rahul
hero.who: a 31-year-old chartered accountant in Ahmedabad who saves every dream for retirement

story.b: Rahul's Diwali leave is cancelled for the third year in a row. Audit season, his manager says, as always. Rahul nods, eats a cold thepla at his desk and answers forty emails before nine at night. His father calls from their village in Kutch. He wants Rahul to come and help with the mango trees, like when he was a boy. Rahul promises to come once things settle down. On the bus home, he scrolls through photos of a college friend trekking in Spiti. He tells himself he will do all of this after retirement, when he has money and time. Then he does the maths. His father is sixty-eight. Retirement is twenty-nine years away. The numbers do not work.

ask.q: Rahul keeps saving every dream for retirement. What is the most useful first step?
o: Keep working hard now and enjoy life fully after sixty
Question why each dream must wait, and pick one to plan for this year
Quit his job immediately to travel and live freely
ask.why: Waiting decades assumes his energy, his father's health and his chances will all still be there. Quitting overnight swaps one extreme for another. Questioning the wait and planning one real experience soon is a practical way to start living now while still working.

chapters.take: Some dreams will not wait until retirement. Plan one sooner.

story.b: Rahul writes down the dreams he keeps postponing. Learning his mother's kadhi from her, properly. Walking the white salt desert at night. Simply sitting with his father among the mango trees. None of them needs a crore of rupees. They need time, maybe a month. He opens the calendar and finds a gap: after the March filing rush, work slows for a few weeks every year. Instead of a rushed four-day trip, he imagines a proper break, a small retirement in the middle of his career, while his father is still strong enough to climb the trees. For the first time in years, the future feels close enough to touch, and Rahul starts planning it in pencil.

ask.q: Rahul wants time with his father but feels a long break is unrealistic. Which plan fits the idea best?
o: Take a proper few-week break during a quieter work period this year
Squeeze in a quick weekend trip once every few years
Wait until he has saved enough to never work again
ask.why: A weekend every few years never gives a relationship the time it needs. Waiting to never work again pushes the dream decades away. A longer break in a quiet season, planned while his father is well, spreads living through his career instead of saving it all for the end.

chapters.take: Spread real breaks through your working life instead of saving them all.

story.b: Now Rahul has to ask his manager for four weeks away, mostly working remotely, and he is scared. He keeps imagining being fired in the meeting. One night, in a notebook, he writes the realistic worst case. His manager says no. Or, at worst, the firm lets him go. Then he writes how he would recover. He has eight months of savings. Three firms in Ahmedabad keep calling him for interviews. He could stay with his parents for a while. Finally he writes what not asking costs him: another year of missed harvests, another year of a father getting older. On paper, the worst case looks temporary and fixable. The cost of staying silent looks permanent.

ask.q: Rahul is still nervous about asking for the break. What should he do next?
o: Avoid the meeting until he feels completely confident
Ask a friend to tell him everything will definitely be fine
Use his written worst case and recovery plan to make the request calmly
ask.why: Waiting for complete confidence can take forever, and a friend's comfort fades by morning. Writing the realistic worst case, how he would recover and what inaction costs turns a vague fear into a clear plan. With that in hand, he can ask calmly.

chapters.take: Fear shrinks when you write the worst case and your way back.

story.h: The list and the red pen
story.b: His manager agrees, on one condition: the March work must be done properly first. Rahul panics and thinks about working faster. Instead, he lists every task from last month. Two big clients brought most of the fees that crossed his desk. Yet he spent hours on a weekly report nobody had opened in months, and on formatting slides for an internal meeting where he only listened. With a red pen, he crosses out the report and offers to share short notes instead of slides. He also sets firm deadlines: each client file closed by Thursday, not whenever. Work that used to fill the whole week now fits into four days. Being busy, Rahul realises, was never the same as being useful.

ask.q: A junior colleague says he is buried in work and plans to stay late daily. What should Rahul advise first?
o: Stay late every day and learn faster typing shortcuts
List his tasks and drop the ones that bring almost no results
Take on extra tasks to show the manager his commitment
ask.why: Speed helps only after the useless work is gone, otherwise he just does unimportant tasks faster. Extra tasks add to the pile. Listing everything and cutting what brings little lets him put his hours where most of the results come from.

chapters.take: Before working faster, stop doing what does not need doing.

story.b: Rahul's phone is still a problem. He belongs to fourteen WhatsApp groups, gets news alerts every ten minutes and answers every email the moment it lands. Each ping breaks his focus on a tax file. So he tries an experiment. He mutes every group except family. He turns off news alerts and reads the paper once, with his morning tea. He checks email at eleven and at four, and tells clients that anything urgent can come by phone. The first day he feels jumpy, as if he is missing something big. By the third day he sees that nothing important was lost. Rahul finishes a client file by lunch, something that used to drag on until evening.

ask.q: Rahul's colleague fears missing something if she stops checking email constantly. What should Rahul suggest?
o: Check at fixed times and give clients a phone route for real emergencies
Keep notifications on but reply a little more slowly
Check email even more often so nothing piles up
ask.why: Slower replies with notifications on still break her focus every few minutes, and checking more often makes it worse. Fixed checking times plus a clear emergency route protect her deep work while making sure truly urgent matters still reach her.

chapters.take: Fewer inputs leave room for the work that matters.

story.b: Two weeks before the break, Rahul looks at what only he can do. Very little, it turns out. He sets automatic reminders for clients' monthly filings, so he no longer types them one by one. He trains Hetal, a sharp junior, to handle routine reconciliations and gives her real responsibility, not just checklists. He tests working from home on Fridays and sends his manager a short summary each evening of what was finished. After three Fridays, the manager stops asking for the summaries. Rahul also sets up an automatic monthly transfer into savings, so the break never touches his rent. Every hour he hands off or automates is an hour he buys back for the mango trees.

ask.q: Rahul worries his manager will not trust him to work from Kutch. What is the smartest approach?
o: Simply announce he will be working remotely and stop explaining
Cancel the plan, since managers never trust remote work
Prove it in small steps, like remote Fridays with clear daily updates
ask.why: Announcing it without proof invites a refusal, and cancelling gives up too early. Small trial days with visible results build trust step by step, so remote work starts to feel safe for the manager as well as freeing for him.

chapters.take: Automate, delegate and build trust step by step to buy back time.

story.b: Weeks later, Rahul is in Kutch. Most mornings he works two focused hours on the veranda, checking email only at eleven, while his father waters the trees. Hetal handles the routine files and messages him just twice in the whole month. In the afternoons, his mother teaches him her kadhi, and he gets it wrong three times before it tastes right. One night, father and son walk out to the white salt flats and sit quietly under the stars. Back in Ahmedabad, nothing falls apart. His manager even asks him to explain how he cut the weekly report. Rahul still works hard. He just no longer believes that living has to wait until sixty.

chapters.take: Living now and working well can go together when you design for it.
